overview: Scentre Group is a Sydney-headquartered, ASX-listed stapled REIT that owns, operates and develops 42 Westfield-branded shopping centres across Australia and New Zealand, located within close proximity to 21 million people. It is a vertically integrated landlord-operator-developer (not just a passive property trust), managing leasing, marketing, security, development and digital/media monetisation across its own portfolio and $51.2 billion of assets under management (Group share ~$34.0 billion) held with 18 joint venture partners across 32 of the 42 destinations.

business_model.summary: Scentre earns predominantly recurring rental income from long-term leases with anchor department stores/discount department stores and thousands of specialty retailers, supplemented by fixed and turnover-linked rent, car park and media/out-of-home advertising income, and fee income for property/leasing/development management of jointly-owned centres. Growth comes from rent escalations (contracted ~4.5% average specialty escalations), positive releasing spreads, occupancy gains, and redevelopment of existing space and adjacent land holdings (>670 hectares) into higher and better uses including residential.

revenue_streams.name: Car parking and other property income
Property, leasing and development management fees (JV assets)

business_model.customer_type: B2B (retail tenants: department stores, discount department stores, supermarkets, ~3,700 specialty business partners across 12,000 outlets) with an underlying B2C customer base of 540m+ annual shopping centre visits
business_model.geographic_mix: New South Wales largest (15 destinations, ~251m visits/yr), Queensland (6), Victoria (7), Western Australia (4), New Zealand (5), South Australia (3), ACT (2) — all Australia/New Zealand, no international diversification

competitive_position.market_position: Largest owner and manager of premium/super-regional shopping centres in Australia and New Zealand; sole operator of the globally recognised Westfield brand in the region since acquiring the rights in 2014

moat_factors.description: Centres sit on scarce, well-located land near major transport hubs in dense catchments; new large-format regional malls are near-impossible to replicate given planning constraints, making the portfolio effectively unassailable by new supply
Globally recognised premium retail brand that attracts flagship international luxury and lifestyle tenants (Chanel, Loewe, Balenciaga, Loro Piana) ahead of competing centres
3,700 business partners and deep leasing relationships give Scentre negotiating leverage, market intelligence and a highly diversified, resilient tenant base; occupancy at 99.8%, highest since 2013

In-house leasing, development, marketing, security and centre-management capability generates fee income from third-party capital (JV partners) and is sought after to manage newly joint-ventured assets
Single 'A' credit ratings from S&P and Moody's provide access to diverse, cost-effective global debt markets (AUD, EUR, USD) even amid a heavy debt-funded balance sheet

weaknesses: High geographic concentration risk (100% Australia/New Zealand, no international diversification)
Elevated balance-sheet gearing (35.5% at H1 2026) versus a REIT sector generally deleveraging
Reputational and safety overhang from the April 2024 Westfield Bondi Junction attack and February 2026 coronial findings critical of security preparedness
Capital-intensive redevelopment pipeline exposes returns to construction cost inflation and execution risk
Reliance on discretionary retail spending, which is sensitive to consumer confidence and interest rates

growth_drivers: Comparable Net Operating Income (NOI) growth ~4.4-4.8% driven by occupancy gains, positive leasing spreads (+3.2% on new specialty deals) and average rent escalations of ~4.5%
$4 billion future retail development pipeline repurposing existing space (e.g. Westfield Bondi Level 6 $240m, Westfield Southland, Westfield Burwood) to improve productivity and mix

Strategic land holding masterplanning: >670 hectares of land with planning proposals lodged for 16,100 dwellings (e.g. Westfield Hornsby up to 53 storeys/2,100+ dwellings, Westfield Belconnen, Westfield Warringah declared State Significant Development)

Capital recycling via joint venturing of assets (~$2.2bn introduced in 2025, plus $882.5m from ART taking a 50% stake in Westfield Mt Gravatt in H1 2026) funding growth without diluting securityholders while retaining management/fee income
Record customer visitation (540m in 2025, +2.7%; 552m annualised through August 2026) and record business partner sales ($30.0bn in 2025, +3.6%; $30.3bn MAT by mid-2026)
Growing Westfield membership base (5.0m members, +11% in 2025) supporting data-driven leasing and media monetisation
Improving cost of debt (5.4% in H1 2026 vs 5.7% prior year) as higher-coupon notes are refinanced, boosting FFO

business.description: Specialty retail sales and turnover rent are exposed to a slowdown in Australian/NZ consumer spending
Online retail continues to compete for share of wallet, though Scentre's experience-led, ~45% experience-based tenant mix and click-and-collect integration have proven relatively resilient

February 2026 coronial findings were critical of Scentre's security contractor preparedness; potential for further reputational damage, regulatory scrutiny, litigation or increased security compliance costs
Department stores such as David Jones have been downsized at several centres, requiring active re-leasing to maintain productivity
Large redevelopment and residential masterplanning pipeline exposed to construction cost inflation, approval delays and partner (e.g. Cbus Property) execution risk

financial.description: Gearing of 35.5% at H1 2026 (up from 30.4% at FY2025) with total debt near $14.9bn; interest cover of 3.6x and FFO-to-debt of 11.9% leave less headroom versus deleveraged peers
Weighted average cost of debt ~5.4%; while ~89-95% of debt is hedged near-term (swap rate ~3.26-3.29%), hedge coverage steps down through 2029, exposing the Group to rate resets on refinancing

Statutory profit is heavily influenced by non-cash investment property revaluations (e.g. FY2025 statutory profit of $1,778.5m vs FFO of $1,187.5m), creating headline earnings volatility unrelated to operating cash flow
New Zealand operations create modest AUD/NZD translation exposure

regulatory.description: Residential masterplanning growth strategy depends on state/local government rezoning and community consultation outcomes that are outside Scentre's control and can be slow or contested
Potential for new mandated security standards for large public venues following the Bondi Junction coronial inquest, raising compliance costs across the portfolio
Any adverse change to stapled-trust or REIT tax treatment in Australia would affect distributable income

macro.description: As a highly leveraged, income-yielding asset class, REIT valuations and cost of capital are sensitive to the RBA cash rate and bond yields; a higher-for-longer rate environment pressures valuations and refinancing costs
A slowdown in Australian/NZ economic growth or employment would reduce discretionary retail spending and put pressure on turnover rent and leasing spreads
Elevated construction costs affect the economics of the $4bn development pipeline and residential masterplanning projects

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australian retail property has stabilised post-pandemic with occupancy at multi-year highs (Scentre at 99.8%, highest since 2013) and positive leasing spreads returning across the sector; large-format, experience-led malls have proven structurally resilient to e-commerce compared to smaller/weaker centres
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate — rental income is largely contracted and defensive, but turnover rent, leasing spreads and asset valuations are cyclical with consumer spending and interest rates
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High — as a leveraged REIT (gearing 35.5%), both cost of debt and capitalisation rates used to value the portfolio are directly affected by interest rate moves

recent_developments.event: H1 2026 results: FFO of $612.4m (+4.4% YoY, 11.73 cps), distributions +4.9% to $481.3m (9.215 cps), comparable NOI +4.4%, occupancy 99.8%, gearing 35.5%, cost of debt improved to 5.4% from 5.7%; management upgraded FY2026 guidance to at least 23.79 cps FFO (+4.25%+) and 18.473 cps distributions
Australian Retirement Trust (ART) introduced as 50% joint venture partner for Westfield Mt Gravatt, generating $882.5 million in new capital

NSW State Coroner released findings on the Bondi Junction Inquest into the 13 April 2024 attack, criticising security contractor preparedness; Scentre stated it is reviewing findings in detail and has already implemented enhanced security measures (control room policy changes, AI trials, paid police presence)

FY2025 annual results: FFO $1,188m (+4.9%, 22.82 cps), distributions $923m (+3.4%, 17.72 cps), statutory profit $1,778.5m, comparable NOI +4.8%, occupancy 99.8% (highest since 2013), record $30.0bn business partner sales (+$1.0bn), 3,090 leasing deals with +3.2% specialty spreads

Introduced ~$2.2bn of new capital via joint venturing, including 50% of Westfield Chermside sold to two Dexus funds for $1.3bn and a 19.9% interest in Westfield Sydney sold to Australian Retirement Trust for $864m at a 4.69% cap rate

Capital management: redeemed $1.0bn Subordinated Non-Call 2026 Notes; issued $650m Non-Call 2031 Subordinated Notes at 2.0% margin, $1.0bn 10-year AUD senior notes at 1.38% margin, and €500m (~$900m) 8-year senior notes at 1.295% margin (return to European market); maintained single 'A' ratings from S&P and Moody's

Completed redevelopments at Westfield Sydney (CHANEL, Moncler, OMEGA), Westfield Southland ($72m, new dining/entertainment precinct), Westfield Burwood ($48m, ALDI/JB Hi-Fi/Nike/rebel) and Westfield Bondi Level 1 ($28m, Virgin Active); commenced $240m Westfield Bondi Level 6 redevelopment

items.notes: Improved from 5.7% in H1 2025; reflects refinancing of higher-coupon legacy notes

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Elliott Rusanow highlighted the fifth consecutive year of earnings and distribution growth, record occupancy (99.8%, highest since 2013) and record customer visitation and business partner sales, framing the strategy around driving visitation, broadening the tenant/business mix, and unlocking additional long-term growth from the Group's substantial land holdings via residential masterplanning. Management pointed to continued strong demand for space and positive leasing momentum as the basis for the FY2026 guidance upgrade, alongside a lower cost of debt from ongoing refinancing.

bull_case: Irreplaceable, scarce super-regional mall portfolio with near-impossible-to-replicate locations provides a structural moat against new supply
Five consecutive years of FFO and distribution growth, with FY2026 guidance just upgraded to at least 4.25% growth off record occupancy (99.8%) and strong leasing spreads

Capital-light growth optionality from a $4bn development pipeline plus >670 hectares of land holdings with 16,100+ dwellings in planning, funded via accretive joint-venture capital recycling rather than new equity
Improving cost of debt (5.4% vs 5.7% a year ago) as legacy high-coupon notes are refinanced, directly boosting FFO

Consensus analyst rating of Buy with price targets averaging ~A$4.03-4.21 (a meaningful premium to the recent ~A$3.6-3.7 share price), reflecting confidence in the growth and capital management trajectory
bear_case: Gearing increased to 35.5% at H1 2026 (from 30.4% at FY2025) and interest cover of only 3.6x leaves less balance-sheet flexibility if rates stay elevated or valuations soften

100% concentration in Australian/NZ retail property offers no geographic diversification, and statutory profit is heavily distorted by non-cash property revaluations, complicating like-for-like performance assessment

Reputational and potential regulatory/security-compliance-cost overhang from the critical February 2026 coronial findings on the Bondi Junction attack, with possible mandated security upgrades across the portfolio
REIT sector valuations and cost of capital remain sensitive to Australian interest rates; a higher-for-longer rate path would pressure cap rates, asset valuations and refinancing costs
Growth increasingly depends on execution of complex, multi-year residential rezoning and masterplanning projects subject to government/community approval timelines outside the company's control
